readerTitle: The partnership clause worth ten times the fee
caseNote: 가상 사례 (IT 지원 회사와 회계 법인의 소개 제휴, 조경 회사와 부동산 관리 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 제휴의 가치와 협상력은 잘될 때의 조건이 아니라 끝날 때의 조건이 정한다. 끝내는 방법은 사이가 좋을 때 정해야 한다.
misconception: 제휴는 수수료와 조건만 잘 협상하면 되고, 끝나는 이야기를 꺼내면 관계가 상한다.

sources.text: 계약·협상 실무의 일반 개념 (종료 조항, 통지 기간, 종료 후 수수료(tail), 인수인계 의무)

factChecks.note: 조경 사례: 매출 $400,000 중 절반 $200,000이 관리 회사에서 나온다는 가정. 90일 통지 기간은 설명용 가정입니다.
종료 조항의 효력, 고객 유치 금지 조항 등은 나라와 계약마다 다릅니다. 카드에서는 법률 조언을 하지 않고 전문가 검토를 권하는 수준으로만 적었습니다.

cards.title: Saving $12,000 can cost you $120,000.
body: An IT support firm signed a referral deal with an accounting firm. It bargained hard over the referral fee and won.
It never asked one question: what happens when this ends?

image.label: Two business people shaking hands over a contract with one blank page
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 두 사람이 악수하는 테이블 위 계약서. 수수료 페이지는 빨간 펜으로 여러 번 고쳐져 있고, 마지막 "Ending" 페이지만 텅 비어 있음. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: Which term matters most?
body: You run an IT support firm. An accounting firm will refer its small-business clients to you. They ask for 15% of what those clients pay you.
You can push hard on one point before signing. Which one?

options.text: Cut the referral fee from 15% to 10%
options.feedback: A real, steady saving. But it protects the money you pay, not the clients you could lose.

options.text: Lock the deal in for five years
options.feedback: It feels safe, but it also traps you if the deal goes bad, and says nothing about what happens at year six.

options.text: Agree in writing what happens to referred clients if either side ends it
options.feedback: Less exciting than a fee cut, but it protects the biggest number in the deal. The next card shows how big.

cards.title: Three years later, the partner leaves.
body: The firm got the fee cut. Three years in, the accounting firm starts its own IT service and tells its clients to switch. The contract says nothing about ending. Half the referred clients follow.
The fee cut saves **$12,000** a year. The silent exit costs **ten times** that.

breakdown.label: Saved each year by the fee cut
Lost each year when half leave

cards.title: Exit terms
body: **Exit terms** are the rules for how a partnership ends: how much notice each side gives, who keeps the customers, whether payments continue, and what help is owed during the handover.
Almost every partnership ends. Owners change, strategies shift, a partner starts competing. The exit terms decide what you still have when that happens.

image.label: A bridge with an exit ramp clearly marked
image.brief: 두 회사 건물을 잇는 다리 일러스트. 다리 중간에 "Exit" 표지판이 붙은 정돈된 진출로가 있고, 진출로 위에 고객 아이콘들이 안전하게 내려옴. 밝고 단순한 플랫 스타일.

cards.title: Four questions to answer before you sign.
body: Write the answers down while both sides are still friendly.
list: **Notice:** how many days before either side can leave?
**Customers:** who keeps the relationships and the contact details?
**Money:** do fees stop at once, or continue on existing customers for a set time?
**Handover:** what does each side owe the customers during the switch?
cards.callout: Easy to agree now. Nearly impossible to agree later.

cards.title: Whoever can leave cheaply sets the terms.
body: Exit terms matter long before the end. In year two, the accounting firm asks for 25% instead of 10%. Leaving would cost the IT firm up to $120,000 a year. It would cost the accountants almost nothing.
So the IT firm pays. The side that loses less by walking away holds the power in every renegotiation.
cards.softwareNote: Software partnerships work the same way. If a platform or app marketplace owns your user relationships and data, it can change its terms at will. Keeping a direct line to your users, and a way for them to export their data, lowers your cost of leaving.

cards.title: Too tight is a problem too.
body: Exit terms that only protect you signal distrust. A partner who can't leave easily may refuse to sign, or quietly invest less in the deal.
Long notice periods cut both ways. They protect you from a sudden exit, and they also keep you stuck in a deal that has gone bad.
Aim for terms both sides can live with. For the legal wording, have a professional review the contract.

cards.title: Now it's a landscaping company.
body: A property manager sends you half your work, about $200,000 a year. Lately they pay 60 days late and keep asking for lower prices. Your contract allows either side to end it with 90 days' notice.

options.text: Stop showing up until they pay, to force better terms
options.feedback: It may get you paid once, but it can break the contract and hurt your name with the building owners you'd want to keep.

options.text: Give notice, do the 90 days well, and use them to replace the work
options.feedback: You keep your reputation and use the notice period as runway. The cost is a hard quarter of selling while still working the old contract.

options.text: Stay, because half your revenue depends on them
options.feedback: It protects this year's revenue, but your dependence is exactly why they keep squeezing. At least start winning other clients now.

cards.title: Agree how it ends while you still agree.
body: The exit terms decide what you keep when a partnership ends, and who holds the power while it lasts.
**Try it today:** pick your most important partner. Write down what would happen to your customers, payments and data if it ended next month.
